## Primitives

### Binary

- Number Systems
  - Hindu-Arabic Numeral System - base 10
  - Sumerians - base 60
  - Maya - base 20
  - Yuki - base 8
- Positional Notation/Radix
  - Decimal - Positional notation with radix 10
  - Binary - Positional notation with radix 2
  - Hexadecimal - Positional notation with radix 16

> The breakthrough was place value + zero, which lets the same digit
> mean different things by position: e.g: 505 5 = five 50 = five tens
> 500 = five hundreds

#### NOT - `~`

- `~` unary ~ (invert operator) is used to perform the bit complement or
  `not` operation.
- we can’t represent a single bit in python but now we can perform it on
  integers.

``` python
x = ctypes.c_uint8(0b01010101)
y = ctypes.c_uint8(~x.value)
z = ctypes.c_int8(~x.value)

f'{x.value = },  {x.value = :08b}'
f'{y.value = }, {y.value = :08b}'
f'{z.value = }, {z.value = :08b}'
```

    'x.value = 85,  x.value = 01010101'

    'y.value = 170, y.value = 10101010'

    'z.value = -86, z.value = -1010110'

#### Two’s complement

- Flip every bit.
- Add 1.

``` python
x = 130
f'{x = :08b}'
flip = (~x) & 0xFF
f'{flip = :08b}'
add1 = (flip + 1) & 0xFF
f'{add1 = :08b}  →  {add1}'
```

    'x = 10000010'

    'flip = 01111101'

    'add1 = 01111110  →  126'

### Byte Ordering

- Endianess
  - Little Endian - Most CPUs today
    - Most significant byte(MSB) goes last
  - Big Endian - TCP/IP protocols
    - Most significant byte(MSB) goes first \> Timelines
- Big Endian - IBM 360(1964)
- Little Endian - PDP-11(1970), Intel 8008(1972), Intel
  8080/8086/x86(1974-1978),

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endianness

#### `to_bytes` - byte order

``` python
a = 16784300
b = -16784300

a_le = a.to_bytes(length=4,byteorder='little',signed=True)
a_be = a.to_bytes(length=4,byteorder='big',signed=True)
b_le = b.to_bytes(length=4,byteorder='little',signed=True)
b_be = b.to_bytes(length=4,byteorder='big',signed=True)
f'{a_le = }, {a_le.hex() = }'
f'{a_be = }, {a_be.hex() = }'
f'{b_le = }, {b_le.hex() = }'
f'{b_be = }, {b_be.hex() = }'
```

    "a_le = b'\\xac\\x1b\\x00\\x01', a_le.hex() = 'ac1b0001'"

    "a_be = b'\\x01\\x00\\x1b\\xac', a_be.hex() = '01001bac'"

    "b_le = b'T\\xe4\\xff\\xfe', b_le.hex() = '54e4fffe'"

    "b_be = b'\\xfe\\xff\\xe4T', b_be.hex() = 'feffe454'"

#### Truthy values

- By default, an object is considered true unless its class defines
  either a `__bool__()` method that returns False or a `__len__()`
  method that returns zero, when called with the object

``` python
arr = array('i',[])
f'{bool(True) = }'
f'{bool(False) = }'
f'{bool(0) = }'
f'{bool(1) = }'
f'{bool(-1) = }'
f'{bool(-3) = }'
f'{bool(arr) = }'
arr.append(10)
f'{bool(arr) = }'
f'{bool(()) = }'
f'{bool([]) = }'
f'{bool({}) = }'
```

    'bool(True) = True'

    'bool(False) = False'

    'bool(0) = False'

    'bool(1) = True'

    'bool(-1) = True'

    'bool(-3) = True'

    'bool(arr) = False'

    'bool(arr) = True'

    'bool(()) = False'

    'bool([]) = False'

    'bool({}) = False'

``` python

if a:
  f'True'
else:
  f'False'
```

### Text

#### Characters

- An encoding is a rule to map characters to numbers.
- interpretation of the byte as text = encoding
- To represent all the languages in the world we now use Unicode.
- String is a sequence of characters, `str` in python use Unicode
  encoding.

``` python
f'{ctypes.c_char(65).value = }'
f'{ctypes.c_char(b'A').value = }'
f'{ctypes.c_char(97).value = }'
f'{ord('A') = }'
f'{chr(65) = }'
print()
f'{chr(35) = }'
f'{chr(64) = }'
f'Size of c_char: {ctypes.sizeof(ctypes.c_char * 8)} bits'
```

    "ctypes.c_char(65).value = b'A'"

    "ctypes.c_char(b'A').value = b'A'"

    "ctypes.c_char(97).value = b'a'"

    "ord('A') = 65"

    "chr(65) = 'A'"

    "chr(35) = '#'"

    "chr(64) = '@'"

    'Size of c_char: 8 bits'
